name: Asclepias

taxonomic_status.kew_note: Kew Plants of the World Online accepts Asclepias L. This learner includes locally verified native species, nonlocal comparisons, and the explicitly introduced tropical milkweed comparison; inclusion does not imply county nativity.

project_scope.project_scope_note: Eleven learner cards including explicit introduced and nonlocal comparisons. Previous six-species project scope is historical.

genus_diagnostics.habit: Mostly perennial herbs in local native set; A. curassavica is an introduced garden species that can behave as a subshrub or annual according to climate.
genus_diagnostics.latex: Most project species produce milky latex; Asclepias tuberosa is the major exception here with clear/watery sap.
genus_diagnostics.inflorescence: Umbel-like milkweed flower clusters, terminal and/or axillary depending on species.
genus_diagnostics.flower: Five reflexed or spreading corolla lobes surrounding a highly specialized gynostegium.
genus_diagnostics.corona: Five hood-like corona structures, usually with species-specific shape; internal horns can be present, reduced or absent. Hoods and horns are not the same thing; both A. viridis and local A. asperula have hoods, but the binary 'asperula horned / viridis hornless' rule is incorrect.
genus_diagnostics.gynostegium: Fused reproductive column with anther wings, stigmatic slits, corpuscula, translator arms, and paired pollinia.
genus_diagnostics.fruit: Follicles containing flattened seeds with silky comas.

high_value_field_traits: Leaf arrangement: alternate, opposite, or whorled
Corona hood shape and length relative to corolla lobes; independently check true horn versus hood

central_texas_quick_key.if: Sap clear/watery rather than milky; flowers usually orange
Milky sap AND leaves needle-thin and obviously whorled around the stem
Leaves broader, opposite/sub-opposite, often wavy; corona hoods unusually long and projecting above the column
Flowers white; leaves opposite and appearing in four ranks
Narrow lanceolate/linear-lanceolate, sharply tapering leaves; often rocky-site clumps, crowded near-spherical umbel; five hoods, but no reliable projecting-horn difference from viridis
Broader oblong/ovate, more blunt-tipped leaves; pale green corolla lobes with shorter purple-tinged hoods; compare corona length relative to corolla lobes

study_notes: Do not identify milkweeds by flower color alone.
The corona and gynostegium are among the highest-value structures for difficult identifications.
Leaf arrangement plus sap type often narrows the locally native subset; this learner additionally includes introduced and nonlocal look-alike cards.
Asclepias subverticillata is treated as a separate species from Asclepias verticillata.

b069_comparison.historical_hold_note: Historical B069 snapshot; A. incarnata range HOLD was resolved later and should not be interpreted as current.

b069_study_strategy.warning: Do not use broad 'Texas native' status as a substitute for exact target-zone county evidence. A. syriaca is not Texas-native under current Kew.

quick_split: A. viridiflora — compact greenish umbels, opposite leaves, local PASS.
A. incarnata — wet-site plant with narrow opposite leaves and pink umbels; historical range HOLD was resolved to PASS in October 2026.
A. speciosa — tall white-tomentose western/northern milkweed with large pinkish umbels; target-zone FAIL.
A. syriaca — tall clonal common milkweed with broad leaves and pink-purple umbels; non-Texas-native comparison.

expanded_quick_reference.look_here_first: Moist site; opposite narrow leaves and conspicuous pink umbels.
Compact greenish upper-axillary flower clusters; inspect reproductive structure vs green milkweed.
Tall woolly western milkweed; broad hairy leaves and big rose-purple umbels; target-zone FAIL.
Tall broad opposite leaves; round pink umbels and stout follicles; target-zone FAIL.
Usually red corolla with bright yellow corona, opposite leaves and milky sap; introduced in Texas.

comparison_cards.title: Green milkweed vs antelopehorns: look at the LEAF first
comparison_cards.look_here_first: First compare mature leaf width and tip shape; then flower corona-to-corolla proportions. Do not call one species 'hoodless' or claim that the presence of a projecting horn is the defining split.

field_matrix.viridis: Mostly broad oblong–ovate; frequently roughly 1–6 cm wide
field_matrix.asperula: Mostly narrow lanceolate–linear-lanceolate; often roughly 0.4–3.7 cm wide

field_matrix.viridis: Five hoods; no projecting horn; tiny internal rudiment may occur
field_matrix.asperula: Five hoods; subsp. capricornu documented without an enclosed horn

field_matrix.viridis: Corona segments shorter than half corolla lobe length (FNA)
field_matrix.asperula: Corona relatively longer by comparison; check flower in same side view

field_matrix.viridis: Crowded terminal, may have a few upper lateral umbels
field_matrix.asperula: Often very crowded terminal hemispherical/globose clusters

field_matrix.viridis: Often deeper prairie/valley soils; spreading or ascending
field_matrix.asperula: Often rocky uplands; ascending to decumbent and clustered

botanical_terms.explain: The five larger pale green petal-like lobes surrounding the center.
One of five cup/pouch-like units making the corona near the flower center.
A separate, sometimes projecting appendage arising within a hood in some Asclepias; not synonymous with the hood.

comparison_cards.caution: Hybrids exist in other parts of the southern Great Plains. No single general photo, growth habit or umbel roundness proves identity.

comparison_cards.ecological_warning: Tropical milkweed is a monarch host but an introduced species. In climates with winter foliage it can facilitate atypical winter breeding and OE spore buildup. Do not count as target native or recommend in local restoration.
